en: What does a baby need more: the one who feeds it, or the one who hugs it?
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
This answer comes from a famous, and pretty uncomfortable, experiment.
In the nineteen fifties, psychologist Harry Harlow raised baby rhesus monkeys away from their mothers.
Each baby got two fake moms.
A wire mom with a milk bottle, and a soft cloth mom with no milk at all.
Back then, many experts believed babies love whoever feeds them.
So the wire mom should win, right?
Nope.
The babies visited the wire mom only to drink.
The rest of the day, they cuddled the soft one.
When a scary toy showed up, they ran straight to the cloth mom and held on tight.
So love wasn't about food.
It was about comfort and touch.
Then came the darkest part.
Some babies were raised completely alone.
Months later, given the two moms, they just curled up and shook.
As adults, many struggled.
Some hid in corners, some attacked others, and some neglected their own babies.
Harlow's lesson was simple.
Babies need touch, movement and play, not just milk.
That was a big deal, because a popular parenting book back then told parents never to hug or kiss their children.
Today, these experiments are seen as cruel, and they fueled the push for better treatment of lab animals.
But they also changed how we raise kids.
Warmth isn't spoiling.
It's a need.
So the hug beats the bottle.
Stay curious!
